$comment: Machine-readable release metrics for arthiqlabs/vedaksha. vedaksha.net fetches this file from raw.githubusercontent so the site stays current without a deploy — before it existed, every engine release needed a matching hand-edit and deploy of the site, and the site drifted twice. Update it in the same commit as a version bump; CI's version-check asserts engineVersion against the tag, so it cannot be silently forgotten. The test counts are the numbers the two CI commands printed at that tag, not an enumeration.

accuracy.$comment: Measured agreement with JPL Horizons (DE441), re-run at the tag rather than carried forward. Published here so the site reads them live like every other figure: they were hand-maintained site constants until 2026-09-01 and had gone unverified from v7.0.0 to v9.1.0. Asserted against the engine's own oracle output by check_metrics_accuracy.py, so they cannot drift from what the tests actually print. The SPK and analytical paths are separately implemented and separately measured - neither figure says anything about the other.
accuracy.quantity: Mean angular residual in apparent geocentric ecliptic longitude (of date) vs JPL Horizons. Not a general position-accuracy figure: the oracle fixture also stores ref_latitude, ref_distance and ref_speed (see oracle_comparison.rs), but none of those enter this number -- longitude only.
accuracy.targetConvention: Comparisons query planetary-system barycentre IDs (Body::naif_id()), matching what the DE440s kernel stores and what SpkReader returns -- not physical planet centres. Querying centres instead would inject a spurious ~0.1 arcsecond offset for the outer planets (scripts/generate_horizons_oracle.py), the same order of magnitude as the headline mean itself.

analytical.$comment: AnalyticalProvider (VSOP87A + ELP/MPP02), no runtime data file, via tests/analytical_oracle.rs.

era.$comment: Both mean/max figures above describe the measured-Delta T era ONLY. Past 2025 both Horizons and delta_t.rs must PREDICT Delta T rather than read it from the IERS record, and the two predictions diverge; the residual out there is time-scale disagreement, not ephemeris error, and scales with each body's angular rate. Quoting a mean over the full 24,350 rows alongside the sub-arcsecond claim overstates it. Never write '24,350 positions ... 0.103 arcsec'.
